Mitch McConnell decided to show up to work this week, ending a 92-day absence
that was one of the biggest middle fingers to Americans from an elected
official that I can remember. Now God is responding in kind, casting McConnell
as the villain in a sad sequel to _The Mummy_.

The wheelchair-bound McConnell was
[hospitalized](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/mitch-mcconnells-dead-line)
on June 14. His office said only that he was "receiving excellent care," and
for the next two weeks that's all we were told. Then on June 30 came the
publication of a 911 call from his Washington home, in which a dispatcher
reported a cardiac arrest and a medic radioed that CPR was in progress. Twelve
days and a wave of public backlash later, McConnell's office finally put out a
statement. He'd only suffered a fall, they claimed, releasing the below
[proof-of-life](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/mitch-mcconnell-releases-
proof-of) photo.

It took all of two days for the embarrassing display that Capitol Hill was
surely dreading. At Wednesday's Senate Agriculture Committee markup of the
Farm Bill, the clerk called McConnell's name and nobody could hear his answer.
Sen. John Hoeven, seated beside him, leaned over and told him to vote "no." A
staffer leaned in from behind. Chairman John Boozman, on his other side, told
him "aye." The clerk had to call his name a second time before McConnell
produced a hoarse but audible "aye."

It was also the only word he'd said on camera since his disappearance.

The 84-year-old Kentucky Senator is in many ways the Godfather and final boss
of the gerontocracy. Though many older members of Congress have finally
decided to retire after enormous public pressure, as I've [written
about](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/the-gerontocracy-is-dead), McConnell
holds on, clearly unable to fulfill his duties but also unwilling to resign.
And not just him: I can't remember the last member of Congress who resigned
mid-term due to health reasons -- despite the fact that six have died in
office this term alone.

If you want to know how he's getting away with this -- amid an eye-popping [71
percent](https://emersoncollegepolling.com/kentucky-2026-poll-barr-maintains-
edge-in-gop-primary-as-booker-gains-among-democratic-voters/) disapproval rate
from Kentuckians in March, _before_ his hospitalization -- one big reason is
that major media have been doing him a solid.

Here's how The New York Times reported his first public appearance to the
press.

"After two years--" McConnell began, correcting himself, the _Times_ wrote:
"two decades -- of dodging your questions, I wasn't sure how many of you would
be here today."

Ha-ha. Get it? He hates addressing the public. Yeah, we picked up on that,
Mitch.

What the Times story didn't mention was that McConnell's staff [barred
media](https://www.thedailybeast.com/mitch-mcconnells-aides-busted-censoring-
his-frail-voice/) from recording video of McConnell's remarks. Nor that
McConnell spoke "slowly and with some difficulty,"
[according](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/14/mitch-mcconnell-
return-senate) to The Guardian.

The funniest part of the Times article is where they recount how McConnell
"seemed to freeze while speaking in public" -- episodes that were caught on
camera in which he clearly froze. Imagine the headline: "Twin Towers Seemed to
Fall."

The Mitch is back. The Office of the Attending Physician, Congress's concierge
medical service, paid McConnell's office a visit yesterday, according to video
[posted by](https://x.com/DesireeReports/status/2100330456545640846?s=20)
independent journalist Desiree Townsend (who broke news of the 911 cardiac
arrest call in the first place, forcing Washington media to address the
scandal).

Why was a doctor needed? Who knows. McConnell's office won't say.

_Correction: This story has been updated to reflect the ambiguity of what
McConnell said when casting his initial voice vote on the farm bill._
